title: Why Do We Sleep?
paragraphs: Humans spend roughly a third of their lives asleep, which raises an obvious question: what does all that time achieve? Sleep researchers and health organisations generally recommend seven to nine hours a night for adults, and considerably more for children and teenagers, whose brains and bodies are still developing.

Rather than being a single uniform state, sleep is organised into cycles of about ninety minutes. Each cycle moves from light sleep into deep, slow-wave sleep and then into REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that accompany it and closely linked to dreaming. Several cycles follow one another over a typical night.

These stages appear to serve different purposes. Deep sleep is associated with physical recovery and with consolidating memories, turning the day's experiences into longer-lasting knowledge. Studies in animals have also shown that the brain clears away waste products more effectively during sleep, a finding that may help explain why sleep matters for long-term brain health.

Missing an occasional night is unlikely to cause lasting harm, but chronic sleep loss has measurable consequences. Attention, memory and judgement decline, emotions become harder to regulate, and over time poor sleep is linked to a higher risk of several health problems. Far from being wasted time, sleep is one of the foundations of a healthy life.
